Question three. How do you process a file too big to fit in memory? Don't call read or read lines. On the same eight megabyte file, read holds the whole text: seventeen megabytes. Read lines holds every line: thirty-four. A file object is already a lazy iterator over its lines, so a plain for loop streams it, in about a hundred fifty kilobytes. Chain generators on it, and nothing is read until the last one asks. Question four. How do you process a large CSV with pandas without loading it all? Pass chunk size to read CSV, and you get an iterator of data frames: ten chunks of a hundred thousand rows. Sum each chunk by group, and fold it into a counter. The totals match the whole-file read exactly, and memory peaks at one chunk: seven and a half megabytes, not fifty-four. Sums add up across chunks. A mean doesn't: the mean of the chunks' means is off. Carry the sum and the count, and divide at the end. That one pass deserves a closer look.

Question five. What's the difference between an iterable and an iterator? An iterable, like a list or a dict, hands out a fresh iterator each time you loop over it. An iterator keeps its place, and once it reaches the end, it's used up. Read the list twice: four rows, then four again. Read the generator twice: four, then zero. A generator is an iterator, and so is an open file. Here's how it bites: count the rows for the log, then load them. Four counted, zero loaded, and no error. For two passes, make a list, or create the generator again. Next, how a set answers without looking.
